subtype: Direct versus indirect communication across cultures [Mismatch]
passage: At the office kitchen I watched Pradeep ask his new colleague Chaitanya, who had just moved from Osaka, whether he'd have time to look at a spreadsheet. "Would you be able to check it today?" Chaitanya paused, then said, "It is a little difficult." Pradeep nodded and walked away, apparently satisfied. An hour later he came back, puzzled, asking why it wasn't done. Chaitanya replied, still politely, "I said it was difficult." I saw them both frown. I don't know what either felt. Later Pradeep asked, "When you say difficult, do you mean not possible?" Chaitanya smiled. "Yes. I'm sorry I didn't say it more plainly." Pradeep laughed. "I'll ask more plainly too."

qa.q: Where had Chaitanya just moved from?
qa.a: He had just moved from Osaka.

qa.q: What did Chaitanya likely mean by "a little difficult", and what might Pradeep have understood?
qa.a: Chaitanya likely meant it was not possible, while Pradeep heard only that it was hard but doable, so they read the same words differently.

qa.q: What could each of them do to avoid such a mix-up?
qa.a: They could ask clarifying questions kindly, such as whether "difficult" means "not possible", and state requests plainly.

qa.q: How might Pradeep have felt when he came back and found the spreadsheet not done?
qa.a: Pradeep was puzzled, and perhaps a little frustrated as his frown suggests, since he thought Chaitanya had agreed, until asking plainly cleared it up.

grounding: An observer sees a direct request and an indirect refusal cross, and the two clear it by asking.

subtype: Direct versus indirect communication across cultures [Mismatch]
passage:
Day one. Ankita had just started at a Dutch design firm and liked how her colleague Jyoti said things plainly: "I don't like this layout." It stung. Ankita, raised to soften every criticism, wondered whether Jyoti disliked her.

Day four. Ankita gave Jyoti her own feedback in her usual way: "It could maybe be even better if the top part had a little more space?" Jyoti frowned and said she didn't understand what to change.

Day nine. They sat down. Ankita said, "Where I'm from, we hint." Jyoti laughed. "Where I'm from, we shout. Tell me the one thing to change and I'll listen." Ankita said, "Move the logo." Both smiled, relieved.

qa.q: What kind of firm had Ankita just joined?
qa.a: She had just started at a Dutch design firm.

qa.q: What was Ankita feeling about Jyoti's plain comment on day one, and what changed?
qa.a: She felt stung and wondered if Jyoti disliked her, and later she realised it was just a different style.

qa.q: What could Ankita and Jyoti each do to work together well?
qa.a: They could ask clarifying questions kindly, and Ankita could name the one thing to change while Jyoti listens for hints.

qa.q: How might Jyoti have felt when Ankita's feedback was full of hints?
qa.a: She probably felt confused about what to change, not offended, since she asked for clarity.

grounding: Ankita and Jyoti meet direct and indirect styles over several days and bridge them by asking.

subtype: Direct versus indirect communication across cultures [Mismatch]
passage: Wasim beta, you've started work with the Gujarati traders, so let Hansa Ba tell you something. When I was twenty-two, I got married and moved from Ahmedabad to my husband's family in Hyderabad. At home, we said things plainly: "I don't like this", "Please do that." In my new home, my mother-in-law never said no. She'd say, "We'll see," or "It's a bit difficult," or she'd just go quiet. I thought she agreed with everything! Then things I'd asked for never happened, and I was hurt. One day my sister-in-law explained: "Ammi hints. 'We'll see' means no." I felt so confused. Then I tried something. When she said "we'll see", I asked gently, "Ammi, shall I take that as a no, or should I ask again next week?" She laughed. "No, beti. Not this time." Neither way is better. Just ask kindly when you're not sure.

qa.q: Where did young Hansa move after her marriage?
qa.a: To her husband's family in Hyderabad.

qa.q: How did young Hansa feel when the things she asked for never happened?
qa.a: She felt hurt and confused, having taken her mother-in-law's hints as agreement.

qa.q: What choice inside the story bridged the difference?
qa.a: Young Hansa gently asked a clarifying question, whether "we'll see" meant no, and her mother-in-law answered plainly.

qa.q: How did Hansa's mother-in-law react to the direct question?
qa.a: She laughed and answered clearly, suggesting she appreciated being asked kindly.

grounding: Shows a young adult meeting someone who hints through politeness and learning to ask clarifying questions kindly.

subtype: Direct versus indirect communication across cultures [Mismatch]
passage: It was the last day of the project handover, and the office in Bengaluru was chaos: two clients calling, a server down. Tejas's new manager, Ankita, who had just moved from the Berlin office, walked up to his desk. "Your report has three errors. Fix them by four." Then she walked off. Tejas sat stunned. At his previous team, a manager would have said, "Maybe we could look at a few small things?" This felt like a slap. He wanted to complain. With forty minutes left, he didn't have time to brood. He fixed the errors. Then he walked to her desk. "Ankita, can I ask something? When you said the report had errors, were you upset with me?" She looked surprised. "No! I was just saying what needed doing. In Berlin that's normal. Should I say it differently?" Tejas smiled. "Maybe add a 'please'. I'll get used to the directness." "Deal," she said.

qa.q: By what time did Ankita want the errors fixed?
qa.a: By four.

qa.q: What was Tejas feeling when Ankita walked off?
qa.a: He felt stunned and hurt, as if slapped, because he was used to softer, indirect feedback.

qa.q: What did Tejas do that helped under time pressure?
qa.a: He fixed the errors first, then kindly asked Ankita whether she was upset, instead of brooding or complaining.

qa.q: How did Ankita see her own direct words?
qa.a: She saw them as just saying what needed doing, normal where she came from, and she was willing to adjust.

grounding: Shows a young adult meeting a direct communicator after working with indirect ones and asking a kind clarifying question.

subtype: Direct versus indirect communication across cultures [Mismatch]
passage: Yusuf and his flatmate Nazia had shared a flat in Mumbai for a month when Yusuf noticed something. Whenever he asked if she minded his cousin staying over, she'd say, "Up to you," and go quiet. When he asked about the music at night, she'd say, "It's fine, it's fine." But she seemed tired and cool afterwards. Yusuf's own family said everything plainly, sometimes loudly. He was confused. Was she angry? Did "fine" mean fine? One Sunday over breakfast, he asked. "Nazia, I think I might be missing your hints. When you say 'up to you', do you actually mind?" Nazia put her cup down and laughed, a little embarrassed. "Honestly? Yes. I grew up where saying no directly is rude." "And I grew up where hints go straight over my head," Yusuf said. They agreed: she'd try saying it plainly, and he'd ask when unsure.

qa.q: How long had Yusuf and Nazia shared the flat?
qa.a: For a month.

qa.q: What was Nazia feeling when she said "Up to you" and went quiet?
qa.a: She was uncomfortable and minded, but felt that saying no directly would be rude.

qa.q: What did Yusuf do that helped?
qa.a: He asked kindly and directly whether her "up to you" meant she minded, instead of guessing.

qa.q: How did Yusuf's own family background shape how he read Nazia?
qa.a: His family said everything plainly, so her hints went over his head and left him confused.

grounding: Shows two young adults with direct and indirect styles finding that neither is better and asking clarifying questions kindly.

subtype: Direct versus indirect communication across cultures [Mismatch]
passage:
In their Bengaluru hostel room, Harsha looked up from a book. "It's quite cold tonight, no?"
Chaitanya didn't look up from the laptop. "Yeah, December."
"Hmm. The window's letting in a lot of wind."
"Mm-hmm."
Harsha pulled the blanket up to the chin and sighed.
Chaitanya finally looked up. "Wait. Are you asking me to close the window?"
"Only if you don't mind. I didn't want to be rude; it's your side of the room."
"Oh! You can just say 'please close the window.' I'd never have guessed."
"At home, if I said it that straight, Amma would say I was ordering people around."
"And at mine, if you hint, nobody notices. My family just says things."
"So what do we do?"
"You try saying it plainly. And if you go quiet and sigh, I'll ask, 'Is there something you'd like?'"
"Okay. Then, please close the window."
Chaitanya closed it, grinning. "See? Nobody died."

qa.q: Which month is it?
qa.a: December.

qa.q: Why did Harsha hint instead of asking directly?
qa.a: Harsha felt uncomfortable being blunt, worried it would seem rude since the window was on Chaitanya's side and plain requests sounded like ordering people around at home.

qa.q: What agreement did they reach?
qa.a: Harsha would try saying needs plainly, and Chaitanya would ask kindly whenever Harsha went quiet or sighed.

qa.q: How did Chaitanya experience Harsha's hints?
qa.a: As ordinary small talk; Chaitanya missed the request at first because in Chaitanya's family people just say things.

grounding: It illustrates a direct speaker and an indirect speaker learning that neither style is better and that kind clarifying questions bridge the gap.
